segments.text: She wakes up in a flooded cabin. The masts are gone. So is the man she was going to marry.
No masts, no engine, nobody? No chance. Let's go back to the start.
Tami Oldham, twenty-three, from San Diego, grew up around boats. Now she's sailing the South Pacific with her fiancé, Richard Sharp, a British sailor.
In Tahiti they're hired to sail a yacht, the Hazana, to San Diego for its owners. About four thousand miles.
On the twenty-second of September, {1983|nineteen eighty-three}, they sail out of Papeete. For two weeks, it's easy.
Then a storm builds to the east, grows fast, and turns their way. For three days they try to outrun it.
On the twelfth of October, it catches them. Hurricane Raymond. Category four. Waves of forty feet and more.
Richard is at the wheel, clipped on. He sends her below. Then she hears him shout: Oh my God.
The yacht is thrown over. She's hurled against the cabin, and everything goes black.
She comes to about twenty-seven hours later, with a gash on her head, in a cabin half full of sea.
On deck, his safety line is still tied on. The ring of his harness has been torn open. Richard is gone.
The radio is wrecked. The emergency beacon is damaged. The engine won't run. She is on her own.
So she fixes what she can. She pumps the cabin out by hand. She takes half of a broken spinnaker pole, about nine feet of it, stands it up as a mast, and hangs a storm jib on it.
Then, a plane. Low, right over her. She waves and yells. It flies on. Later, two ships pass, too far away to see her.
So where now? With this rig, San Diego is out of reach. Hawaii is the closest land. Fifteen hundred miles.
She has a sextant. With the sun at noon she finds her latitude. Her plan: sail north to nineteen degrees, then turn left, and run west to Hawaii.
To know how far west she is, she needs the time. About a week in, she finds her watch in the bilge.
She lives on tins, rationed. She writes in the log every day. At night, she sleeps with one of his shirts.
And all the way, she said later, she heard Richard's voice, urging her on.
On the twenty-second of November, day forty-one, a Japanese research ship finds her just outside the harbour at Hilo, Hawaii, and tows her in.
The head injury leaves her unable to read for years. In {2002|two thousand and two}, she tells it all in a book, Red Sky in Mourning. In {2018|twenty eighteen}, it becomes a film, Adrift.
She married, had two children, and still sails. Round her neck she wears a small sextant.
Richard Sharp was lost in that storm. She steered a wreck fifteen hundred miles, alone. I said no chance. I was wrong. Case closed.
